content: Iodine is an essential trace element that plays a critical role in the synthesis of thyroid hormones, specifically thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3). These hormones are vital for regulating metabolism, growth, and development. In regions where dietary iodine intake is insufficient—commonly in remote inland areas where marine foods are not consumed—iodine deficiency can lead to the development of goiter, also known as endemic goiter. This condition is characterized by the enlargement of the thyroid gland. Additionally, severe iodine deficiency can result in cretinism, a condition associated with significant developmental delays, intellectual disabilities, and other health complications. To address iodine deficiency in such areas, small amounts of iodine are often added to table salt in the form of sodium iodide, potassium iodide, or potassium iodate. This fortified product is referred to as iodized salt. In some cases, iodine compounds are also incorporated into other food products, such as flour, to further combat deficiency in affected populations.
